title: Baba Ramdev's 'Ayurvedic Hookah' Ignites Memes, Mockery and a Medical Warning
excerpt: A viral video shows the yoga guru loading a hookah with herbs and claiming it balances the doshas. Doctors say inhaling any smoke is no therapy.
body:
• A video posted on Baba Ramdev's Instagram account shows the yoga guru preparing what he calls an "Ayurvedic hookah" — a traditional brass hookah loaded with herbs including liquorice, turmeric, mustard seeds, carom seeds and camphor — and suggesting it can balance the body's three doshas.
  • The clip has gone viral, drawing a wave of memes, jokes about "ayurvedic hukka bars" replacing club nights, and sharp criticism from users who call the claims misleading.
  • Health experts caution there is no clinical evidence that inhaling herbal smoke is a safe or effective treatment for cough, congestion or any other ailment, and warn smoke inhalation can irritate airways and worsen respiratory conditions.
  • The "ayurvedic hookah" is not a commercial product and neither Ramdev nor Patanjali has issued any statement on the video or its health claims.

Only Baba Ramdev could turn a hookah into a health claim. The yoga guru has set social media ablaze after a video posted on his own Instagram account showed him preparing what he calls an "Ayurvedic hookah" — a traditional brass hookah loaded not with flavoured tobacco but with a mix of herbs he suggests can balance the body's doshas.

In the clip, Ramdev places mulethi (liquorice) into the hookah's upper chamber, telling the camera "Isme saari jari butiya hai" — "this has all the herbs." He adds turmeric, mustard seeds, carom seeds, kakda singi and desi camphor, then declares "Ye hukkah ban gaya" — the hookah is ready. He then suggests a woman standing beside him inhale the smoke, claiming it can balance the three Ayurvedic doshas — vata, pitta and kapha — and offer relief from cough and nasal congestion, according to reporting by LiveMint.

The memefest

The video spread rapidly, and the internet responded the way it always does with Ramdev: with jokes. "Ab saare club or pub me Baaba Ramdev ka hukka," one user wrote, playing off the famous 'Hookah Bar' Bollywood song. Others joked that the day "ayurvedic hukka bars" replace regular hookahs in clubs isn't far off, and one quipped, "Ab wo din dur nhi jab Herbal daru ayega" — the day when alcohol too will be made from herbal ingredients. Summing up the mood, netizens declared: "Bas yahi baaki tha" — only this was left.

""Ab saare club or pub me Baaba Ramdev ka hukka," one user wrote, playing off the famous 'Hookah Bar' Bollywood song."

Not everyone was laughing. "Waiting for the Supreme Court to finally hold this fraud baba accountable and teach him a lesson once and for all," one critic wrote on X, while another user called the concoction "more toxic than smoking a cigarette."

What doctors say

Medical experts and fact-checkers say the health claims don't hold up. There is no strong clinical evidence that inhaling smoke or vapour from such herbal preparations is a safe or effective treatment for cough, nasal congestion or any other illness. Smoke inhalation — whatever the ingredients — can irritate the airways and may worsen respiratory conditions, especially in children, the elderly, and people with asthma or chronic lung disease.

The warnings on tobacco, flavoured hookahs and vaping apply regardless of "herbal" framing: inhaling smoke into the lungs carries risks that no herb list can erase. The clip has surfaced at a moment of rising concern about hookah and vaping culture among young Indians, which makes a viral endorsement from one of the country's most recognisable wellness figures especially consequential.

Not a product — yet

For now, the "ayurvedic hookah" exists only as a viral video. It is not available for purchase, and neither Ramdev nor Patanjali has issued any statement about the clip or the claims made in it. That silence matters: Ramdev has prior form here. The Supreme Court previously rebuked him and Patanjali over misleading health advertisements, and any commercial product making therapeutic claims would face immediate advertising-scrutiny.

Separately, a Haridwar-based Ayurvedic college is researching a nicotine-free "herbal cigarette" with 15 Ayurvedic herbs as a potential smoking-cessation aid — but researchers there say data is still being collected and no conclusions can be drawn. Ramdev's hookah demonstration is unrelated to that research.

The line between tradition and marketing

Some supporters defended the video as rooted in tradition, arguing that smoke was used as treatment in ancient Bharat. There is a grain of history there — Ayurvedic texts do describe dhumapana, therapeutic smoke inhalation — but practitioners note the classical procedure is highly specific, dosage-bound and practitioner-guided, nothing like a casual hookah session in a club.

That gap — between a classical ritual and a viral hookah video — is exactly what critics say Ramdev keeps exploiting: dressing mass-market spectacle in the authority of ancient medicine. Whether Patanjali clarifies, disowns or doubles down will tell whether this was a guru's kitchen experiment or the soft launch of another product line.
image_caption: Yoga guru Baba Ramdev in a still from the viral Instagram video showing his so-called ayurvedic hookah. Medical experts say inhaling any smoke is not a safe therapy for cough or congestion, despite the herbal ingredients.
nri_angle: Ramdev's Patanjali products have a large diaspora following; diaspora families navigating Ayurveda-meets-wellness-trend claims need clear medical context on what's tradition and what's marketing.
